F1.quote: This study updates the ILO’s 2023 Global Index of Occupational Exposure to Generative AI (GenAI), incorporating recent advances in the technology and increasing user familiarity with GenAI tools.
F1.claim: the study defined by its authors: an update of the ILO's 2023 Global Index of Occupational Exposure to GenAI, for advances in the technology and users' growing familiarity
F1.lineage: what it is: the ILO's index of occupational exposure to GenAI, refined

F2.quote: This ILO Working Paper refines the global measurement of occupational exposure to generative AI by combining task-level data, expert input, and AI model predictions.
F2.claim: the ILO's page: the working paper refines the global measurement of occupational exposure to GenAI from task-level data, expert input and AI model predictions
F2.lineage: what it is: the ILO's index of occupational exposure to GenAI, refined

F3.locus: the brief's page, heading and lede
F3.quote: Research Brief Generative AI and jobs: A 2025 update This brief summarizes an ILO Working paper that refines the global assessment of occupational exposure to generative AI.
F3.claim: the research brief 'Generative AI and jobs: A 2025 update' summarizes the working paper
F3.lineage: what it is: the ILO's index of occupational exposure to GenAI, refined

F4.quote: The ILO–NASK Index was developed to better understand how generative AI may affect work at the task level.
F4.claim: NASK's page names it the ILO–NASK Index, built to understand how GenAI may affect work at the task level
F4.lineage: what it is: the ILO's index of occupational exposure to GenAI, refined

F5.quote: the Research department of the ILO has partnered with NASK, the National Research Institute of the Ministry of Digital Affairs in Poland, to develop a more precise assessment of potential effects of GenAI on employment across countries.
F5.claim: the makers: the ILO's Research department in partnership with NASK, the National Research Institute of Poland's Ministry of Digital Affairs
F5.lineage: the makers: the ILO, NASK and the authors

F6.quote: Authors Who prepared the report? NASK Analysis and Research Office … it played an active role in the preparation of this report.
F6.claim: NASK's page: the report prepared by the NASK Analysis and Research Office, the ILO having 'played an active role in the preparation'
F6.lineage: the makers: the ILO, NASK and the authors
F6.checked_against: saved text B4.txt (sha256 998ee35dd2c9f7eb…), whitespace-normalised; multi-part quote joined by ' … ', each part checked

F7.quote: Author(s) Pawel Gmyrek Janine Berg Karol Kamiński Filip Konopczyński Agnieszka Ładna Balint Nafradi Konrad Rosłaniec Marek Troszyński
F7.claim: the ILO's page lists eight authors, Balint Nafradi among them
F7.lineage: the makers: the ILO, NASK and the authors

F8.quote: Paweł Gmyrek Janine Berg Karol Kamiński Filip Konopczyński Agnieszka Ładna Konrad Rosłaniec Marek Troszyński Abstract
F8.claim: the working paper's own title block lists seven authors, without Balint Nafradi
F8.lineage: the makers: the ILO, NASK and the authors

F9.quote: This study builds on the method developed by the ILO (Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond, 2023 - GBB hereafter) , which used task descriptions from the 4-digit International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) and the GPT-4 model to estimate task-level and occupational scores of exposure to GenAI technology
F9.claim: its lineage: the 2023 method of Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond, ISCO-08 task descriptions scored with GPT-4

F10.locus: card title (video, 11m; unreachable: no URL found)
F10.quote: Generative AI and Jobs: A global analysis of potential effects on job quantity and quality.
F10.claim: an ILO video card under the title of the 2023 working paper, the predecessor

F11.quote: Using a representative sample from the 29,753 tasks in the Polish occupational classification system and a survey of 1,640 people employed in each 1-digit ISCO-08 groups, we collect 52,558 data points regarding perceive potential of automation for 2,861 tasks.
F11.claim: the survey: 1,640 people employed in Poland scored a representative 2,861 of the 29,753 Polish tasks, 52,558 data points
F11.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F12.quote: This means that tasks of managers are assessed by individuals working as managers, tasks of professionals are assessed by professionals, etc.
F12.claim: each occupational group's tasks scored by people working in that group
F12.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F13.quote: relying on three advanced LLMs available on the market at the end of 2024: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5.
F13.claim: the first, purely algorithmic scoring by three LLMs, GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5
F13.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F14.quote: a score ranging from 0 to 1 for each individual task, where 0 means the task cannot be automated and 1 means the task could be fully automated with GenAI technology (the task can be conducted without participation of a human operator).
F14.claim: the score defined: 0 a task that cannot be automated, 1 a task that could be fully automated, conducted without a human operator
F14.lineage: the unit: a task's automation score, an occupation's mean and spread, four gradients

F15.quote: We then compare this input with a survey and several rounds of Delphi-style discussions among a smaller group of international experts.
F15.claim: the workers' scores compared with an expert survey and Delphi-style rounds
F15.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F16.quote: While the experts are expected to have familiarity with the current family of generative AI technologies and their applications, expertise in AI design or development is not a requirement.
F16.claim: the experts chosen for knowledge of labour markets and tasks; AI design expertise not required, since technology experts tend to overstate capacities
F16.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F17.quote: Based on this process, we create a repository of knowledge about task automation that goes beyond national specificities and use it to develop an AI assistant able to predict scores for tasks in the technical documentation of ISCO-08.
F17.claim: the human scores built into a repository from which an AI assistant predicts scores for ISCO-08's tasks
F17.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F18.quote: the correlation between predictions based on ISCO-08 tasks and Polish 6-digit tasks is 0.92, demonstrating exceptional stability of predictions.
F18.claim: predictions from ISCO-08 and from the Polish tasks correlate at 0.92, which the authors call exceptional stability
F18.lineage: method: workers scoring tasks, experts, LLMs, a predictor

F19.quote: we rely on two moments of distribution: occupational mean and standard deviation (SD) of task-level scores pertaining to a given 4-digit occupation.
F19.claim: an occupation classed by two moments of its task scores, mean and standard deviation
F19.lineage: the unit: a task's automation score, an occupation's mean and spread, four gradients

F20.quote: Gradient 4 highlights occupations with the highest share of tasks exposed to potential GenAI-driven automation, and with a high consistency of this exposure across tasks (Highest exposure, low task variability).
F20.claim: Gradient 4 defined: the highest share of tasks exposed to potential automation, consistently across tasks (Table 5: mean ≥ 0.6 and mean − SD ≥ 0.5)
F20.lineage: the unit: a task's automation score, an occupation's mean and spread, four gradients

F21.quote: Defines four progressively increasing gradients of GenAI exposure depending on the mean exposure score and the degree of task variability for each ISCO-08 occupation.
F21.claim: the brief: four gradients by mean score and task variability
F21.lineage: the unit: a task's automation score, an occupation's mean and spread, four gradients

F22.quote: we focus on the 112 occupations identified as exposed and estimate the share of employment that these occupations represent at the global, regional, and income-based levels.
F22.claim: employment shares estimated for the 112 exposed occupations, globally, by region and by income group, on the ILO's global estimation model
F22.lineage: the unit: a task's automation score, an occupation's mean and spread, four gradients

F23.quote: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category, albeit with significant differences between female (4.7%) and male employment (2.4%).
F23.claim: one in four workers worldwide in an exposed occupation; 3.3% of employment in the highest gradient, 4.7% of female and 2.4% of male
F23.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F24.quote: These differences increase with countries’ income (9.6% female vs 3.5% male in Gradient 4 in HICs), and so does the overall exposure (11% of total employment in LICs vs 34% in HICs).
F24.claim: exposure rises with income, 11% of employment in low-income against 34% in high-income countries; Gradient 4 in high-income countries 9.6% female, 3.5% male
F24.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F25.quote: However, when disaggregated by gender, 28% of male employment is exposed, with only 3.5% in gradient 4, compared to 41% of female employment, with 14.4% in gradient 3 and 9.6% in gradient 4.
F25.claim: in high-income countries 41% of female against 28% of male employment exposed
F25.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F26.quote: Gender disparities are also more pronounced in wealthier regions, particularly in Europe and Central Asia, where 39% of female employment falls into one of the four exposure gradients compared to 26% for men.
F26.claim: in Europe and Central Asia 39% of female against 26% of male employment exposed
F26.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F27.quote: These patterns reflect both occupational structures and the extent to which GenAI-exposed roles, such as clerical, financial, and customer service jobs, are concentrated in higher-income countries.
F27.claim: the patterns by income and sex reflect occupational structures and where exposed roles are concentrated
F27.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F28.locus: 'Exposure is gendered and worse in wealthier economies' ¶2
F28.quote: This reflects the gendered distribution of clerical and customer-facing roles, which are both more exposed and more common among female workers.
F28.claim: The People Space: the gender gap reflects the gendered distribution of clerical and customer-facing roles
F28.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F29.quote: This difference is shaped by infrastructure, digital access and workforce structure.
F29.claim: The People Space: the income difference is shaped by infrastructure, digital access and workforce structure
F29.lineage: findings: shares of employment exposed, by income and sex

F30.quote: In addition, the 2023 estimate attributed 13% of employment as subject to “augmentation” and an additional 16.2% of employment in “the big unknown”. The combined employment share for Gradients 1-3 for the world in the current analysis is 20.5%, 9 percentage points lower than combined shares of augmentation and “the big unknown” (29.2%) reported in 2023.
F30.claim: against 2023: Gradients 1–3 hold 20.5% of world employment, against 2023's 13% augmentation and 16.2% 'big unknown', 29.2% together

F31.quote: Clerical occupations continue to have the highest exposure levels. Additionally, some strongly digitized occupations have increased exposure, highlighting the expanding abilities of GenAI regarding specialized tasks in professional and technical roles.
F31.claim: clerical occupations still the most exposed; some strongly digitized professional and technical occupations more exposed than in 2023

F32.quote: Among the 13 occupations classified in gradient 4, the majority represent clerical roles, including data entry clerks, typists and word processing operators, accounting and bookkeeping clerks, and general office clerks.
F32.claim: 13 occupations in Gradient 4, most of them clerical

F33.quote: some occupations – such as financial analysts, and web and multimedia developers (gradient 4), as well as bank tellers, translators, applications programmers, investment advisers (gradient 3) – have increased their levels of exposure
F33.claim: rising: financial analysts and web and multimedia developers (Gradient 4), bank tellers, translators, applications programmers, investment advisers (Gradient 3)

F34.quote: the highest exposure to GenAI is typically observed among groups with the largest share of tasks of cognitive nature and it declines with tasks of physical nature, which are more prominent among occupational groups 4-9 (Figure 2).
F34.claim: exposure highest where tasks are cognitive; it declines with tasks of physical nature

F35.quote: our 2023 scores for such tasks, which reached 0.9 in some cases, reflected an overly optimistic assessment of full automation potential. In reality, many of these tasks still require substantial human effort.
F35.claim: a revision of its own 2023 scores for clerical tasks: overly optimistic about full automation

F36.quote: Overall, the automation scores are slightly lower than in 2023 (a mean automation score of 0.29 in 2025 versus 0.30 in 2023), though the variability of scores is considerably lower (standard deviation 0.14 in 2025 v. 0.30 in 2023).
F36.claim: mean score 0.29 against 0.30 in 2023; standard deviation 0.14 against 0.30

F37.quote: Growing abilities of GenAI models in such areas as voice, image and video generation have increased automation scores for a range of tasks in media- and web-related occupations.
F37.claim: scores raised for media- and web-related tasks by voice, image and video generation

F38.quote: As most occupations consist of tasks that require human input, transformation of jobs is the most likely impact of GenAI.
F38.claim: transformation of jobs the most likely impact, since most occupations hold tasks that require human input
F38.lineage: transformation over redundancy, and its qualification

F39.quote: One in four workers across the world are in an occupation with some degree of GenAI exposure, but because of the continued need for human input, most jobs will be transformed rather than made redundant.
F39.claim: the brief: most jobs will be transformed rather than made redundant
F39.lineage: transformation over redundancy, and its qualification

F40.quote: Indeed, the results indicate that few jobs consist of tasks that are fully automatable with current GenAI technology; nearly all occupations have some tasks that require human input.
F40.claim: few jobs consist of fully automatable tasks; nearly every occupation has tasks requiring human input
F40.lineage: transformation over redundancy, and its qualification

F41.quote: However, this does not mean that demand for these occupations will remain stable, as the efficiencies gained from introducing technology may mean that fewer workers are needed.
F41.claim: the qualification: demand for these occupations may still fall, since efficiencies may mean fewer workers
F41.lineage: transformation over redundancy, and its qualification

F42.quote: The purpose of the ILO–NASK Index is not to predict the disappearance of jobs, but to identify where work is most likely to change.
F42.claim: NASK: the index's purpose is to identify where work is most likely to change, not to predict the disappearance of jobs
F42.lineage: transformation over redundancy, and its qualification

F43.quote: It is important to stress that these new estimates reflect “exposure” to GenAI and not the actual impact on employment. As in 2023, the 2025 estimates represent the upper threshold of the percentage of employment that could be affected if GenAI technology were fully implemented.
F43.claim: the stated limit: exposure, not the actual impact on employment; an upper threshold, if GenAI were fully implemented
F43.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F44.quote: Infrastructure constraints (electricity, broadband), insufficient digital skills, the cost of technology, and inherent operational difficulties associated with the technology are just some of the barriers to full adoption.
F44.claim: barriers to full adoption: infrastructure, skills, cost, operational difficulty, and acceptance
F44.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F45.quote: Finally, the estimates do not account for new jobs that may be created, nor the technological advances that could potentially automate more tasks in the future. In that sense, our estimates present a static snapshot of the exposure of existing occupations to GenAI at the start of 2025.
F45.claim: no new jobs and no future advances counted: a static snapshot at the start of 2025
F45.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F46.quote: we stress that such exposure does not imply the immediate automation of an entire occupation, but rather the potential for a large share of its current tasks to be performed using this technology.
F46.claim: exposure is not the immediate automation of an occupation but the potential for a large share of its tasks
F46.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F47.quote: We stress that these classifications merely suggest the general trends and types of occupations at different levels of exposure, since any type of task scoring system carries a degree of subjectivity.
F47.claim: the gradients suggest general trends only; any task scoring carries subjectivity
F47.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F48.quote: One of the limitations of the current approach is that neither ISCO-08 nor the Polish classification system includes information on the relative frequency or importance of tasks within occupations. As a result, all tasks are weighted equally when calculating exposure scores.
F48.claim: a stated limit: all tasks weighted equally, the classifications carrying no frequency or importance of tasks
F48.lineage: the stated limits: exposure not impact, an upper threshold, a snapshot

F49.quote: On the downside, this survey design means that the sample may not represent the entire working population, and interpretability of opinions on the automation potential is limited to comparisons within each 1-digit group.
F49.claim: the survey's stated limit: the sample may not represent the working population; opinions comparable only within each 1-digit group
F49.lineage: the stated limits of the survey: Poland, the sample, the match

F50.quote: For 91.5% of the tasks, respondents did not report performing a similar task in their work
F50.claim: for 91.5% of tasks, respondents did not report performing a similar task
F50.lineage: the stated limits of the survey: Poland, the sample, the match

F51.locus: §2 Tasks and occupations in the 6-digit system in Poland ¶1
F51.quote: it seems reasonable to assume that Poland is representative of the upper threshold of automation potential, due to high availability of digital equipment and widespread internet access.
F51.claim: Poland assumed representative of the upper threshold of automation potential
F51.lineage: the stated limits of the survey: Poland, the sample, the match

F52.quote: The new global index presented in this paper is generic, due to the nature of ISCO-08 and the structure of tasks associated with occupations in this framework.
F52.claim: the index is generic, by the nature of ISCO-08; its strength a common global denominator
F52.lineage: the stated limits of the survey: Poland, the sample, the match

F53.quote: As argued by numerous economists, the key to unlocking the productivity benefits of GenAI lies not in the search of outright labour savings, but in the extent to which human expertise can be complemented with new technological capacities to reshape occupations and generate additional value-added
F53.claim: gains, as economists argue (Acemoglu, Autor): productivity benefits lie in complementing human expertise, not in outright labour savings
F53.lineage: gains, direction and transition: what the index says of them

F54.quote: A key question – largely dependent on the policies shaping this evolution – is to what extent these jobs can retrain and retain existing workers, rather than drive labor churn through workforce replacement and the recruitment of typically younger specialists
F54.claim: whether digitized jobs retrain and retain workers or churn them through replacement depends on the policies shaping the change
F54.lineage: gains, direction and transition: what the index says of them

F55.quote: there is need to ensure that the transition is managed through social dialogue, both to minimize “technological unemployment” and the hardship associated with it
F55.claim: the transition to be managed through social dialogue, to minimize 'technological unemployment'
F55.lineage: gains, direction and transition: what the index says of them

F56.quote: Workers know their jobs best and can play an important role in the design, adaptation and use of the technology at the workplace, to the benefit of both working conditions and productivity.
F56.claim: workers know their jobs best and can shape the technology's design and use
F56.lineage: gains, direction and transition: what the index says of them

F57.quote: Linking our refined index with national micro data enables precise projections of such transformations, offering a foundation for social dialogue and targeted policy responses to manage the transition.
F57.claim: its use: linked to national microdata, a foundation for social dialogue and policy
F57.lineage: gains, direction and transition: what the index says of them

F58.quote: In addition, we make all task-level scores publicly available, which also makes it possible for researchers to organize the occupational exposure in different ways than our proposed framework of exposure gradients.
F58.claim: all task-level scores public (pgmyrek.github.io), so others can organize exposure differently

F59.claim: NASK's page offers the full dataset as CSV
